title: The role of social media in spreading misinformation about covid-19 in the levant region (Shatnawi & Ayhan, Jadara Journal for Studies and Research, 8, 2022)
screen_reason: Online survey of 6,910 social-media users in Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine and Syria (June-December 2020). Table 4 and the text report the share of respondents who have read COVID-19 information that turned out to be misinformation: 81.6% ever, with a frequency breakdown (once 16%, a few times 43.6%, many times 22%, never 18.4%). That is a self-reported share of respondents who encountered misinformation, with an explicit denominator - RECALL exposure.

estimates.country: Levant region: Jordan (30.3%), Lebanon (27.2%), Palestine (23.4%), Syria (19.1%)
estimates.platform: Social media platforms (the survey is framed around social media as a COVID-19 information source; Table 4 is titled 'Misinformation about Covid-19 on social media')
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have read information about COVID-19 that turned out to be misinformation (any occurrence)
estimates.denominator: 6,910 valid respondents (7,553 submitted; incomplete or illogical responses removed) recruited as a convenience/snowball online sample of social-media users in Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine and Syria via WhatsApp and social media (smartsurvey.co.uk)
estimates.definition: Respondent indicated having read information about COVID-19 which then turned out to be misinformation, on a four-point frequency scale; the numerator is everyone except the 'Never' category.
estimates.misinfo_def: "In the context of this study, misinformation refers to all fake news and information that promotes false stories on various topics in order to gain high levels of participation on social media platforms, and this information is created to influence the masses, their opinions, attitudes, and behaviors in favor of a specific political party."
estimates.source_quote: To measuring personal experiences about misinformation, the researcher asked participants to indicate whether they have read information about Covid-19 and then it turns out that it is misinformation. While over a half of respondents (81.6%) indicated having encountered this sort of information. 43.6% saw a few times (2-4), 22% Many times (5 or more), and 16% just Once a time. But 18.4% indicated not having encountered this sort of content. as shown in Table 4.
estimates.page_loc: Section 4 Results and discussions, p. 392; Table 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report on a single four-point frequency item; no external verification of any item the respondent had in mind. The questionnaire had nine items, was reviewed by field specialists and pre-tested on a small sample; the paper additionally reports an 89% agreement rate computed with the 'Azuroff & Mayer equation' for a 'content analysis tool', although no content analysis is reported anywhere in the study.
estimates.moderator_quote: We picked a Convenient Sample targeting social media users because of the various audience characteristics, and the sample was acquired using the snowball method. Quantitative research was used to collect data for this study. Although 7553 responses were submitted, only 6910 were chosen for the study. Between June and December 2020, respondents were contacted via WhatsApp and placed on social media sites via smartsurvey.co.uk.
estimates.notes: denom_scope=population (survey rule). 81.6% is stated VERBATIM twice in the text, so it is kept under R8 even though it is also the complement of the verbatim 18.4% 'Never' cell. NOT split by country: the paper reports the four countries only as sample composition and never breaks the 81.6% down by nation, so a pooled multi-country row is the only defensible coding. platform_norm=multi_platform rather than survey because the question sits inside a social-media-framed instrument and Table 4 is explicitly titled 'Misinformation about Covid-19 on social media', although the item wording itself does not name a platform - a coding an adjudicator may reasonably flip to 'survey'. The paper contains several sloppy statements (calling 81.6% 'over a half', calling 29.2% 'third' then 'second', mislabelling the first column of Tables 3 and 4 'Level of Education', and Figure 6 percentages in the text (73/37/28) not matching the figure labels (28/37/37)); none of these affect Table 4, whose four cells sum exactly to 6,910.

estimates.notes: Strict-threshold variant of the 81.6% row (same denominator, same instrument, higher frequency cut-point), kept because the protocol accepts 'how often' scales when a share above a threshold is given. Do NOT pool this row together with the 81.6% row - they are the same respondents at two thresholds. 1,520/6,910 = 22.0%, matching the verbatim 22%.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED, with reasons: (1) TRUST ITEM. 'Most of the responses 77.4% answered sometimes only, 20% never but gives you the general picture, and just 2.6% all the time' to the question whether social-media platforms report trustworthy information. The 20% 'never [trustworthy]' cell is arguably a perception-of-misinformation-in-one's-environment measure, which the protocol would count; but the item asks about TRUSTWORTHY information rather than misinformation, and 'never but gives you the general picture' is a compound response option, so I judged it too far from a misinformation share to code. An adjudicator may want it as a perceived-environment row. (2) 55% use social media as their main COVID-19 information source, 52% local media, 45% WHO, 35% international media - source-use shares, not misinformation. (3) 73% say misinformation increased their panic and fear, 37% increased safety precautions, 28% indifferent - effects, not prevalence (and these text values conflict with the figure labels). (4) Reasons for using social media (61%, 53%, 32%, 23%) and all demographic distributions - not misinformation shares. (5) The 78% figure attributed to Yased (2020) for Algeria is a value the paper CITES from another study, excluded per R8. (6) No breakdown of the 81.6% by country, platform, age or gender is reported, so no sub-rows are derivable.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey, convenience sample recruited by snowball through WhatsApp and social media (smartsurvey.co.uk), June-December 2020, targeting social-media users in Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine and Syria; 7,553 responses received, 6,910 retained after removing incomplete or illogical replies; nine-item questionnaire reviewed by field specialists and pre-tested on a small sample; analysis descriptive (Excel, SPSS 20). No sampling frame, no response rate, no weighting to population benchmarks, no country-level analysis, and self-selection into a social-media-recruited sample means the denominator over-represents heavy social-media users, young people (33.1% aged 18-25) and the highly educated (58.3% bachelor's, 22% postgraduate). The reported 89% agreement statistic refers to a 'content analysis tool' that does not correspond to any analysis presented.
